result:
The client side is standard Inertia and needed no change — the fix is entirely server-side.

`PostController.update()` was hand-rolling its redirect response with a literal `status: 302`, unlike `store()` and `destroy()` which both go through `this.redirect()`. Guren's `Controller.redirect()` picks the status from the request method — 302 for GET, 303 for anything else — and 303 is what matters here: a 302 answer to a PUT tells the browser to replay the *same method* against the new URL, so the follow-up went `PUT /posts/<id>` back into `posts.update`, which answered 302 again, looping until the client aborted with `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` — after the row had already been written, which is why the edit appeared on a manual reload. I replaced the hand-built `Response` in `app/Http/Controllers/PostController.ts:96` with `return this.redirect(\`/posts/${post.id}\`)` plus a short comment on why the status matters, bringing it in line with the other mutating actions; validation still throws before the redirect, so 422 responses on the edit form are untouched. I also added `tests/PostUpdate.test.ts`, which migrates the test database, creates an author and a post, and asserts that a signed-in PUT answers 303 with `Location: /posts/<id>` while an empty payload still answers 422. `bun run typecheck` is clean and `bun test` passes 4/4 across the three test files.
